claims.text: The relevant baseline is a W–Cu architecture with tungsten adjacent to a copper component that is typically CuCrZr.
VFeTiTaW can be introduced as an interlayer between tungsten and copper regions.
A thermal interlayer is needed between tungsten and CuCrZr because of the gradient between their working temperatures.
The VFeTiTaW interlayer increases the effective thermal conductivity of the W–Cu composite.
The VFeTiTaW interlayer preserves the mechanical durability of the W–Cu composite.
The VFeTiTaW interlayer preserves the irradiation resistance of the W–Cu composite.
The proposed application involves high thermal flux conditions characteristic of fusion-reactor divertors.
VFeTiTaW has been studied after annealing at 1100 °C, 1300 °C, and 1500 °C.
VFeTiTaW has been subjected to Ar+, He+, and D+ irradiation in prior testing.
Annealing causes phase growth in VFeTiTaW, with more pronounced growth at higher temperatures.
The VFeTiTaW layer acts as an engineered transition zone at the tungsten–copper interface.
The VFeTiTaW transition zone improves interfacial bonding between tungsten and copper.
The VFeTiTaW transition zone facilitates efficient phonon transmission across the tungsten–copper interface.
Grading the tungsten–copper interface with VFeTiTaW reduces thermal boundary resistance.
Reduced thermal boundary resistance enhances phonon coupling and heat-transfer efficiency.
VFeTiTaW possesses sufficient intrinsic microstructural stability under annealing and irradiation to preserve composite performance.
VFeTiTaW exhibits lower deuterium retention.
Interlayer thickness must be optimized to prevent the interlayer's intrinsic thermal resistance from negating the benefit.
Thermal exposure beyond the studied range may cause degradation or phase instability.

Relative to an otherwise comparable control, the interlayer composite should show a statistically significant conductivity increase with no decrease in strength, fracture toughness, or irradiation performance.
